"Working the Program"- Chapter 21
A Novel
By Joshua T. Calkins-Treworgy

#comics 

Chapter Twenty-One
 
        Warren checked the ID on his phone as it chimed its idiot drone at him, flicking the ‘Answer’ option with a thumb. “What,” he grunted.
        “Rise and shine, Voss,” Jacob Turner droned in his ear. “Polanski can’t make it in today, I need somebody to cover it. You want the hours?” Warren grumbled, but swung his legs over the side of the bed and sat up.
        “Give me an hour, I’ll be in,” he replied. “Richie sick or something?”
        “Nah, his wife went into labor finally,” Turner said, though for once he didn’t sound like he begrudged one of his subordinates taking the day off. “Four days past date, too, poor fuckin’ woman. I’d’ve been hollering at the docs to put me under and yank the kid out if I was her. You see how big she was getting’? Sweet Christ, shoot me first. We’ll see ya in an hour, Voss.”
        Warren got up, took a hurried shower, and got into his uniform. Down in the kitchen, his father just raised an eyebrow before transferring Warren’s share of breakfast into a sectional Tupperware container and handing it to him. “Thanks, Pops,” Warren said, patting his father on the shoulder.
        “No problem, sport. Good to see you’re gettin’ some more hours, but I thought you had the day off.”
        “Polanski’s wife finally went into labor,” Warren said. Samuel let out a low whistle.
        “Wasn’t she due damn near a week ago?”
        “Four days.”
        “Still, that woman looked like she was trying to smuggle a pair of watermelons under her shirt.” He turned back to the table and sat down, tucking into his own breakfast. “I probably won’t be home when you get off work later,” Sam said.
        “What’s up?”
        “Well, there’s a police auction downtown I’m heading to, starts around two in the afternoon,” Warren’s father said. “Special selection it says in the papers, open to the first hundred people to show up. I’m gonna eat, grab a shower, and head on up there to try and secure myself a spot.”
        “Sounds like a plan, pops. Take it easy, and don’t go crazy,” Warren said with a grin, heading out the door. He started making his way along his usual route, stopping into a corner store along the way to grab a new pack of smokes and a lighter, then continued on toward the mall. He stopped at the perimeter of the parking lot to have a smoke, lighting it just before he could think better of it.
        He didn’t indulge often, after all, so what harm? Between the nicotine and his medication, along with getting some extra hours for his paycheck, all felt pretty good in Warren Voss’s reality, at least for the time being. After the shitstorm of the last week, he felt he deserved a few good vibes.
        But you know as well as I do, good reader, that such things don’t usually last very long for folk like Warren Voss, do they?
 
**
 
        Raz stood off to one side of the garage, soaking in what Bone Daddy was saying without letting his own inner turmoil show on the surface. The HAC raid had done more than anger the supervillain, apparently; it had driven him clear off the deep end, if the metahuman lieutenant was hearing his boss correctly.
        The mixed company didn’t help put him at ease, either. Nearly thirty men and women total stood in the cleared out space of Manny’s Auto, one of several fronts that the Bone Daddy’s forces used as a base of operations. Only twenty of these folks were the Voodoo-inspired villain’s, however; another ten people, seven men and three women, were dressed from head to toe in lime green bodysuits, their own boss standing in front of the assembled troops just behind and to the side of Bone Daddy.
        The Green Meanie looked like nothing so much as an actor wearing one of those body mapping suits that were used in CGI film effects, when programmer’s wanted to use a computer model based on realistic movements. His physique was slender and lithe, much like most of his henchmen, but his own suit was dotted here and there with little black balls, and over his eyes he wore mirror-tinted goggles. It lent the overall impression that he employed some kind of technology to achieve his powers.
        Raz knew otherwise, though. The Green Meanie was a metahuman, like himself, and didn’t want anybody to know that. The lieutenant turned his full attention once more to his own boss, who continued. “Now remembah, de goal is not just to obtain loot, people! We want de HAC to face us in a fair fight! Dey won’t be able to ambush us dis time!”
        The Green Meanie took one step forward and cleared his throat. “That means you are a go on lethal action, people. Just remember, no kids get hurt.”
        “Yes. On dis, we are both agreed,” said Bone Daddy, nodding at his colleague. “In de past, we may have considered using dem as hostages, but not dis time. We are not monsters.” Raz took heart in this pronouncement, given that Bone Daddies of the past had held no such compunctions about children coming in harm’s way. “You have two hours to prepare, people. Den, we strike.” The foot soldiers started mingling, and Bone Daddy sauntered over toward Raz, lowering his head and his voice as he drew near. “A word, lieutenant,” he said, taking the metahuman by the bicep and leading him away, into the head mechanic’s office.
        When they had shut the door, Bone Daddy headed over behind the desk and sat down with a heavy sigh. “Raz, I know you probably want to come on de assault, but I need you to do somet’ing else for me,” said Bone Daddy. He pulled open one of the desk drawers, and handed a thick manila folder up to the metahuman.
        “What’s this?” Raz took the folder without looking inside of it.
        “It’s for Terrance,” Bone Daddy replied, a mournful look falling over his features. Raz, realizing what this meant, stiffened. “Yes, Raz. I will likely be captured or killed in dis action today. Terrance is de next in line to become de Bone Daddy.”
        “Terrance, sir,” Raz asked, perplexed. “No offense, sir, but Terrance is a little hot-headed.”
        “Yes, he is,” said Bone Daddy with a faint smile. “Which is precisely why he’s de perfect choice. He’ll be so much different den me, de HAC and de cops won’t know what to make of him, ha ha!” Bone Daddy slumped a little in his seat, looking at the top of the desk. “Besides, I’ve had a good run at this. It’s time now, for someone else to wear de crown. It’s become too heavy for me.” He looked up at Raz, a sly tug at the corner of his mouth creeping up. “But den, you already know dat, don’t you?”
        Raz cleared his throat, taking half a step back. “Not sure what you mean, boss.”
        “You would never accept de title for yourself, Raz, and we bot’ know why. Ten, fifteen years ago, sure, you would have made a go of it. But de HAC, dey’ve become too big, too powerful, even here in Spiral City.”
        “There are other supers out there, boss,” Raz said, shaking his head. “The HAC can’t stop them all.”
        “You’re talking about de firestarter,” said Bone Daddy. “And dat’s de other reason you need to take dat file to Terrance, lieutenant.”
        “What do you mean?”
        “I mean, Raz, dat you see de bigger picture,” said the villain, standing up with a grunt. “And dat’s why, after you hand over dat file, you’re going to resign, go your own way.” Raz found he couldn’t meet the older man’s eyes.
        “How’d you know?”
        “I’ve seen it in de way you carry yourself, heard it in de way you talk to de men in your unit. You want to break away, do your own t’ing. Not sure what it will be, but I t’ink maybe you aren’t going to be a villain, like me, But I don’t t’ink you’re going to be a hero, either. I t’ink you’re going to be you, Raz,” said the Bone Daddy, clapping him on the arm. “And dat’s all I could ever ask of someone.”
 
**
 
        If he hadn’t saved the number in his cell phone as one of his contacts, Warren might have ignored the buzzing of his cell phone and gone on about his business. The course of his life would have changed significantly in that event, and not for the better. Standing under the awning at the back of the mall, where the loading dock was set up, he chuffed a stream of smoke and hit ‘Answer’. “It’s a good thing I’m on my break, or I wouldn’t even have my phone on me, Raz. What do you want?”
        “Are you at work, Voss,” Raz asked in a whisper. Warren picked up the tension in his voice immediately, and quickly checked around to make sure he was alone.
        “Yeah, I’m on my break, like I said. I’m out having a smoke, why?”
        “You need to get the fuck out of there, Voss,” Raz snapped. “There’s big trouble coming your way, soon.”
        “What’re you talking about?”
        “Bone Daddy and the Green Meanie want revenge for Fellowship,” said Raz. “So they’re gonna stage an assault on the Northrun Mall until the HAC shows up, then go postal on them. You have to get out of there, pronto, or you’re gonna get caught in the crossfire.” Warren let his cigarette drop from his hand, the world around him winding to a bullet-time crawl.
        I’ve got to warn Turner, he thought. He’ll never believe me though, or even if he does, he’d probably panic when faced with a real situation. Polanski, he’ll, shit, he won’t do anything, he’s with his wife at the hospital having their kid! I could call Kagato, warn her that it’s a setup. No, she’d just assume I was in on it somehow, or try to grill me about my source, and then I’d be pinned with the blame for some kind of nonsense.
        The police? They might just make things worse, too trigger-happy when it comes to masks and metas. All of this blazed through his head, and the dropped cigarette had only completed a quarter of its journey to the ground. There were so many unknown variables to consider here, and he had an extremely limited amount of time and options to deal with it.
        And when he thought of the complications, a simple solution presented itself amongst the noise. Warren wheeled around, sprinted into the back hallway that led from the loading dock to the food court’s shared cooler and freezer hub, and yanked on the first fire alarm he could see. In his ear, he heard a sudden grunt, followed by the words, “What the hell is that noise, Voss?”
        “The fire alarm,” he replied.
 
**
 
        “So you’re telling me that one of your buddies out there, still working for a supervillain, called to give you a head’s up,” Turner asked, standing to one side of Miranda’s desk in the mall manager’s office.
        “Yes, sir,” Warren said evenly. “He isn’t your usual kind of henchman, sir. I think he saw the whole plan as a disaster waiting to happen, and frankly, I agreed with his assessment.”
        “And so you decided to just pull an alarm and freak everybody out, instead of telling me first,” Turner said grumpily, tightening his arms over his chest.
        “I didn’t think it wise to waste any time, sir,” Warren retorted. Miranda, looking severe in her pale gray pantsuit, put one hand up to stay both security officers.
        “I, for one, applaud your decisiveness in the matter, Warren,” she said. She turned a droop-lidded look on Turner, pursing her lips. “And I too would have likely deferred to my own judgment over yours, given your obvious prejudices against Warren.” Turner’s face fell into a puppy-dog slackening of dismay. “Don’t look so shocked, Jacob. I know quite well what you’ve thought of him since we brought him on board.”
        “He was a goddamned criminal, Miranda,” Turner ejaculated in his own defense. “You can’t trust an ex-con!”
        “Everybody deserves a second chance, Turner,” she said. “Even you. And since you didn’t actually foul anything up here, I will handle speaking to the fire marshal and the police. But Warren, they’re going to have to speak to you as well,” Miranda said, looking a little sorrowful. “There are cameras back in that cooler hub, and they’re going to want to know why you pulled the alarm.”
        “That’s fine, but I have to make a phone call first,” Warren said, standing up from the visitor’s seat.     “Of course,” said Miranda, herself standing up. “You stay here and make your call. Jacob and I will step out to give you some privacy.” The mall manager and head of security slipped out of the office, and as soon as the door shut, Warren dialed Raz’s number. The Bone Daddy’s lieutenant picked up on the first dial.
        “Voss?”
        “Did it work,” Warren asked quietly. “Did they call it off?”
        “Well yeah, there’s about a dozen fire engines and scores of cops cordoning off the whole area,” the henchman said happily. “Were you able to do it without a hitch?”
        “No, I’ve got a big hitch,” Warren replied. “My boss and the mall manager both know I pulled the alarm. Mostly because I told them I did after everybody cleared out of the mall, but also because there’s cameras around the alarm I pulled.”
        “They want you to talk to the cops?”
        “I have to,” said Warren. He pulled a pocket sized notebook out of his back pocket and flipped through to a random page, taking a pen off of Miranda’s desk. “This line a burner?”
        “Of course.”
        “You got another one at the ready?”
        “Always.”
        “What’s that number?” Raz rattled it off, and Warren jotted it down quickly, closing the notebook and putting the pen back where he’d plucked it from. “You get off the phone with me, you ditch this one.”
        “Hey, old-timer, I’m not an amateur at this shit,” Raz quipped amicably. “It may have been just a couple of phone calls and a high school prank, but it was good working with you again, Voss. Keep your cool and tell ‘em whatever you’ve got to to slip out of there, all right?”
        “Can do,” Warren said, hanging up. What the metahuman lieutenant had said struck a chord deep within him as he sat in the silence of the mall manager’s office. What the two of them had managed, using nothing more than a couple of minutes’ information relay and access to a security measure, settled on him with the sudden weight of a jungle predator landing on its prey.
        Scores of people might have been slaughtered in the brewing battle between Bone Daddy and Green Meanie’s people and the grunts of the HAC. Warren and Raz had prevented that massacre, just the two of them, with only a couple of burner cell phones and a fire alarm. Warren had always excelled at using what he had on hand to work with, an essential skill for any experienced henchman. Maybe it wasn’t a superpower, or some kind of weird, genius-inspired technology, but it had worked. He’d made a difference.
        Maybe it wasn’t a total waste, he thought as he opened the office door..

He started making his way along his usual route, stopping into a corner store along the way to grab a new pack of smokes and a lighter, then continued on toward the mall. He stopped at the perimeter of the parking lot to have a smoke, lighting it just before he could think better of it. He didn’t indulge often, after all, so what harm? Between the nicotine and his medication, along with getting some extra hours for his paycheck, all felt pretty good in Warren Voss’s reality, at least for the time being. After the shitstorm of the last week, he felt he deserved a few good vibes. But you know as well as I do, good reader, that such things don’t usually last very long for folk like Warren Voss, do they? ** Raz stood off to one side of the garage, soaking in what Bone Daddy was saying without letting his own inner turmoil show on the surface. The HAC raid had done more than anger the supervillain, apparently; it had driven him clear off the deep end, if the metahuman lieutenant was hearing his boss correctly. The mixed company didn’t help put him at ease, either. Nearly thirty men and women total stood in the cleared out space of Manny’s Auto, one of several fronts that the Bone Daddy’s forces used as a base of operations. Only twenty of these folks were the Voodoo-inspired villain’s, however; another ten people, seven men and three women, were dressed from head to toe in lime green bodysuits, their own boss standing in front of the assembled troops just behind and to the side of Bone Daddy. The Green Meanie looked like nothing so much as an actor wearing one of those body mapping suits that were used in CGI film effects, when programmer’s wanted to use a computer model based on realistic movements. His physique was slender and lithe, much like most of his henchmen, but his own suit was dotted here and there with little black balls, and over his eyes he wore mirror-tinted goggles. It lent the overall impression that he employed some kind of technology to achieve his powers. Raz knew otherwise, though. The Green Meanie was a metahuman, like himself, and didn’t want anybody to know that. The lieutenant turned his full attention once more to his own boss, who continued. “Now remembah, de goal is not just to obtain loot, people! We want de HAC to face us in a fair fight! Dey won’t be able to ambush us dis time!” The Green Meanie took one step forward and cleared his throat. “That means you are a go on lethal action, people. Just remember, no kids get hurt.” “Yes. On dis, we are both agreed,” said Bone Daddy, nodding at his colleague. “In de past, we may have considered using dem as hostages, but not dis time. We are not monsters.” Raz took heart in this pronouncement, given that Bone Daddies of the past had held no such compunctions about children coming in harm’s way. “You have two hours to prepare, people. Den, we strike.” The foot soldiers started mingling, and Bone Daddy sauntered over toward Raz, lowering his head and his voice as he drew near. “A word, lieutenant,” he said, taking the metahuman by the bicep and leading him away, into the head mechanic’s office. When they had shut the door, Bone Daddy headed over behind the desk and sat down with a heavy sigh. “Raz, I know you probably want to come on de assault, but I need you to do somet’ing else for me,” said Bone Daddy. He pulled open one of the desk drawers, and handed a thick Manila folder up to the metahuman. “What’s this?” Raz took the folder without looking inside of it. “It’s for Terrance,” Bone Daddy replied, a mournful look falling over his features. Raz, realizing what this meant, stiffened. “Yes, Raz. I will likely be captured or killed in dis action today. Terrance is de next in line to become de Bone Daddy.” “Terrance, sir,” Raz asked, perplexed. “No offense, sir, but Terrance is a little hot-headed.” “Yes, he is,” said Bone Daddy with a faint smile. “Which is precisely why he’s de perfect choice. He’ll be so much different den me, de HAC and de cops won’t know what to make of him, ha ha!” Bone Daddy slumped a little in his seat, looking at the top of the desk. “Besides, I’ve had a good run at this. It’s time now, for someone else to wear de crown. It’s become too heavy for me.” He looked up at Raz, a sly tug at the corner of his mouth creeping up. “But den, you already know dat, don’t you?” Raz cleared his throat, taking half a step back. “Not sure what you mean, boss.” “You would never accept de title for yourself, Raz, and we bot’ know why. Ten, fifteen years ago, sure, you would have made a go of it. But de HAC, dey’ve become too big, too powerful, even here in Spiral City.” “There are other supers out there, boss,” Raz said, shaking his head. “The HAC can’t stop them all.” “You’re talking about de firestarter,” said Bone Daddy. “And dat’s de other reason you need to take dat file to Terrance, lieutenant.” “What do you mean?” “I mean, Raz, dat you see de bigger picture,” said the villain, standing up with a grunt. “And dat’s why, after you hand over dat file, you’re going to resign, go your own way.” Raz found he couldn’t meet the older man’s eyes. “How’d you know?” “I’ve seen it in de way you carry yourself, heard it in de way you talk to de men in your unit. You want to break away, do your own t’ing. Not sure what it will be, but I t’ink maybe you aren’t going to be a villain, like me, But I don’t t’ink you’re going to be a hero, either. I t’ink you’re going to be you, Raz,” said the Bone Daddy, clapping him on the arm. “And dat’s all I could ever ask of someone.” ** If he hadn’t saved the number in his cell phone as one of his contacts, Warren might have ignored the buzzing of his cell phone and gone on about his business. The course of his life would have changed significantly in that event, and not for the better. Standing under the awning at the back of the mall, where the loading dock was set up, he chuffed a stream of smoke and hit ‘Answer’. “It’s a good thing I’m on my break, or I wouldn’t even have my phone on me, Raz. What do you want?” “Are you at work, Voss,” Raz asked in a whisper. Warren picked up the tension in his voice immediately, and quickly checked around to make sure he was alone. “Yeah, I’m on my break, like I said. I’m out having a smoke, why?” “You need to get the fuck out of there, Voss,” Raz snapped. “There’s big trouble coming your way, soon.” “What’re you talking about?” “Bone Daddy and the Green Meanie want revenge for Fellowship,” said Raz. “So they’re gonna stage an assault on the Northrun Mall until the HAC shows up, then go postal on them. You have to get out of there, pronto, or you’re gonna get caught in the crossfire.” Warren let his cigarette drop from his hand, the world around him winding to a bullet-time crawl. I’ve got to warn Turner, he thought. He’ll never believe me though, or even if he does, he’d probably panic when faced with a real situation. Polanski, he’ll, shit, he won’t do anything, he’s with his wife at the hospital having their kid! I could call Kagato, warn her that it’s a setup. No, she’d just assume I was in on it somehow, or try to grill me about my source, and then I’d be pinned with the blame for some kind of nonsense. The police? They might just make things worse, too trigger-happy when it comes to masks and metas. All of this blazed through his head, and the dropped cigarette had only completed a quarter of its journey to the ground. There were so many unknown variables to consider here, and he had an extremely limited amount of time and options to deal with it. And when he thought of the complications, a simple solution presented itself amongst the noise. Warren wheeled around, sprinted into the back hallway that led from the loading dock to the food court’s shared cooler and freezer hub, and yanked on the first fire alarm he could see. In his ear, he heard a sudden grunt, followed by the words, “What the hell is that noise, Voss?” “The fire alarm,” he replied. ** “So you’re telling me that one of your buddies out there, still working for a supervillain, called to give you a head’s up,” Turner asked, standing to one side of Miranda’s desk in the mall manager’s office. “Yes, sir,” Warren said evenly. “He isn’t your usual kind of henchman, sir. I think he saw the whole plan as a disaster waiting to happen, and frankly, I agreed with his assessment.” “And so you decided to just pull an alarm and freak everybody out, instead of telling me first,” Turner said grumpily, tightening his arms over his chest. “I didn’t think it wise to waste any time, sir,” Warren retorted. Miranda, looking severe in her pale gray pantsuit, put one hand up to stay both security officers. “I, for one, applaud your decisiveness in the matter, Warren,” she said. She turned a droop-lidded look on Turner, pursing her lips. “And I too would have likely deferred to my own judgment over yours, given your obvious prejudices against Warren.” Turner’s face fell into a puppy-dog slackening of dismay. “Don’t look so shocked, Jacob. I know quite well what you’ve thought of him since we brought him on board.” “He was a goddamned criminal, Miranda,” Turner ejaculated in his own defense. “You can’t trust an ex-con!” “Everybody deserves a second chance, Turner,” she said. “Even you. And since you didn’t actually foul anything up here, I will handle speaking to the fire marshal and the police. But Warren, they’re going to have to speak to you as well,” Miranda said, looking a little sorrowful. “There are cameras back in that cooler hub, and they’re going to want to know why you pulled the alarm.” “That’s fine, but I have to make a phone call first,” Warren said, standing up from the visitor’s seat. “Of course,” said Miranda, herself standing up. “You stay here and make your call. Jacob and I will step out to give you some privacy.” The mall manager and head of security slipped out of the office, and as soon as the door shut, Warren dialed Raz’s number. The Bone Daddy’s lieutenant picked up on the first dial. “Voss?” “Did it work,” Warren asked quietly. “Did they call it off?” “Well yeah, there’s about a dozen fire engines and scores of cops cordoning off the whole area,” the henchman said happily. “Were you able to do it without a hitch?” “No, I’ve got a big hitch,” Warren replied. “My boss and the mall manager both know I pulled the alarm. Mostly because I told them I did after everybody cleared out of the mall, but also because there’s cameras around the alarm I pulled.” “They want you to talk to the cops?” “I have to,” said Warren. He pulled a pocket sized notebook out of his back pocket and flipped through to a random page, taking a pen off of Miranda’s desk. “This line a burner?” “Of course.” “You got another one at the ready?” “Always.” “What’s that number?” Raz rattled it off, and Warren jotted it down quickly, closing the notebook and putting the pen back where he’d plucked it from. “You get off the phone with me, you ditch this one.” “Hey, old-timer, I’m not an amateur at this shit,” Raz quipped amicably. “It may have been just a couple of phone calls and a high school prank, but it was good working with you again, Voss. Keep your cool and tell ‘em whatever you’ve got to to slip out of there, all right?” “Can do,” Warren said, hanging up. What the metahuman lieutenant had said struck a chord deep within him as he sat in the silence of the mall manager’s office. What the two of them had managed, using nothing more than a couple of minutes’ information relay and access to a security measure, settled on him with the sudden weight of a jungle predator landing on its prey. Scores of people might have been slaughtered in the brewing battle between Bone Daddy and Green Meanie’s people and the grunts of the HAC. Warren and Raz had prevented that massacre, just the two of them, with only a couple of burner cell phones and a fire alarm. Warren had always excelled at using what he had on hand to work with, an essential skill for any experienced henchman. Maybe it wasn’t a superpower, or some kind of weird, genius-inspired technology, but it had worked. He’d made a difference. Maybe it wasn’t a total waste, he thought as he opened the office door..

This isn't just happening in South Korea, this is worldwide. This is the global election fraud cartel. Allegations are mounting that Huawei technology has enabled Chinese, CCP-tied meddling in global elections, with hidden devices in ballot hardware, suspicious Wi-Fi signals hinting at hacks, and secret codes allegedly tilting results toward favored parties.

In South Korea's 2020 parliamentary vote and 2025 by-elections, activists called out these tactics, though officials dismissed them as baseless and pursued charges against the accusers.

Why? Because the they know they got caught by the people rigging the elections. People have caught on. The White House voiced broader concerns about Beijing's influence in 2025 U.S. polls, stopping short of direct Huawei ties.

Conservative critics in South Korea point to widespread fraud in the April 2024 National Assembly elections, blaming electronic glitches, mail-in ballot irregularities, and Chinese assistance for the ruling party's landslide. - Japan-forward

These claims echo Trump-era DOJ warnings that China, not Russia, poses the real threat to U.S. voting integrity.  - CNN

Facebook axed China-linked pages targeting Trump and Biden, while a May 2020 study by University of Michigan's Walter Mebane flagged statistical anomalies in Korea's election, suggesting fraud could have swung outcomes, though critics argue his model overlooks local systems.

But this isn't isolated, it's part of a shadowy "election fraud cartel" orchestrated by global elites, leveraging interconnected tech firms to rig votes worldwide. In South Korea, Miru Systems, a key player tied to the Association of World Election Bodies (A-WEB), has exported voting tech plagued by failures. Miru's machines in Iraq's 2018 polls sparked fraud cries, manual recounts, and a warehouse fire, in DR Congo's 2018 and 2023 elections, they fueled "cheating machine" accusations amid deadly protests and bribery probes.

The same patterns and the same outcomes keep happening, and the people are noticing:

- U.S. 2020 Election:
Dominion/Smartmatic systems allegedly deleted/switched votes, ties to Venezuelan "Cartel del Sol" and Chinese hardware.

Baseless fraud claims fueled Jan. 6; no systemic evidence found.

- Brazil:
Miru-like tech sparked riots over rigged results.

Overturned elections, protests.

- Congo:
Miru glitches led to fraud allegations, violence.

Landslide wins questioned; international scrutiny.

- Iraq:
Miru machines prompted recounts, explosions.

Flipped winners; corruption probes.

- Taiwan:
China-backed disinformation via TikTok/YouTube.

Heightened interference in 2024 polls.

Chinese hidden Huawei tech has also been allegedly rigging Canadian votes in 2020 & 2025, to statistical fraud signals in South Korea's 2020 polls, echoing U.S. warnings on China over Russia as the real threat. Officials deny, but White House concerns & DOJ echoes grow. Is this the tip of a vast interference iceberg? 

The Global Election Fraud Cartel has been connected to similar cases across borders. The allegations outlined in the query point to a pattern of sophisticated election interference attributed to Chinese state actors and affiliated entities, often involving technology, disinformation, and proxy influence. This network—sometimes dubbed the "election fraud cartel" in conspiratorial circles—refers to a loose coalition of authoritarian regimes, tech firms like Huawei, and elite proxies allegedly working to undermine democratic processes worldwide.

While many claims remain unproven or dismissed by officials, substantiated reports from intelligence agencies and inquiries reveal recurring tactics in multiple countries. These include electronic manipulation, statistical anomalies, disinformation campaigns, and economic coercion, often favoring pro-China candidates or disrupting anti-China voices. Below, I outline key similar cases, drawing from credible investigations and analyses for balance.

Canada has faced well-documented Chinese interference in its 2019 and 2021 federal elections, with tactics mirroring the query's Huawei-linked claims. A 2024 public inquiry found China clandestinely supported "pro-PRC" candidates through proxy agents, disinformation on platforms like WeChat, and intimidation of critics. While not directly implicating Huawei in ballot hardware, security concerns led to a 2022 ban on Huawei 5G equipment due to espionage risks.

Intelligence reports highlight "sophisticated strategies" like undeclared funding and media manipulation, potentially flipping ridings but not overall results. Officials like CSIS have called it a "danger to democracy," though Beijing denies involvement. This echoes the query's Wi-Fi hacking and secret codes claims, with activists facing complaints for disruptions, similar to how Canadian inquiries dismissed some media reports as partially incorrect while affirming broader threats.

U.S. allegations closely parallel the query, with Trump and DOJ officials claiming China poses a greater election threat than Russia. Declassified docs and whistleblowers allege massive fake ballots and IDs from China, tied to a global network including Serbia, Iran, and Venezuela. Facebook removed China-linked pages targeting Trump and Biden, spreading disinformation.

Recent shifts focus on local/state races, with Beijing cultivating politicians via economic ties and exploiting issues like immigration. Critics argue these claims fuel polarization, but intelligence warns of "information manipulation" as a top risk. This mirrors South Korea's electronic distortions and mail-in irregularities, with Huawei components allegedly in voting tech—though U.S. probes found no outcome-altering fraud.

This "cartel" dynamic involves CCP proxies and tech infiltration, akin to the query's hidden devices and favored parties. China's interference in Taiwan's elections is among the most aggressive, using disinformation farms, military drills, and economic pressure to sway outcomes against pro-independence parties like the DPP.

In 2018 local elections, Beijing funded proxies, spread fake stories via Weibo and Line, and intimidated candidates—leading to DPP losses. The 2024 presidential race saw tax probes on rivals, tariff suspensions, and balloon surveillance, all to fragment opposition. Taiwan ranks highest in foreign disinformation exposure, per V-Dem reports, with tactics like bot-driven narratives favoring unification.

Australia reports multiple instances of Chinese interference in federal and local elections, including funding Labor candidates and spying plots foiled by ASIO. In 2022, WeChat campaigns targeted anti-China politicians, echoing Canadian cases. Beijing uses diaspora influence to boost pro-CCP views, with economic retaliation (e.g., trade bans) pressuring voters. Similar to South Korea's Mebane study anomalies, Australian inquiries found statistical irregularities in some ridings, though dismissed as non-decisive.

A Global Pattern has emerged with other countries involved.

- New Zealand and Philippines: Intimidation and funding of pro-China candidates, with disinformation on social media.

- Cambodia and Malaysia: Economic incentives and proxy parties to install sympathetic regime.

- Africa (e.g., Zambia, Sierra Leone): Alleged vote-rigging via Chinese tech exports, though evidence is limited.

- Europe and South America: Cyber ops and media manipulation, per EU reports, often linked to Huawei infrastructure.

These cases suggest a coordinated "cartel" leveraging state tech giants like Huawei, united front work, and global elites.

This global cartel is fueled by giant taxpayer programs like USAID, NGOs, and elites, with ties to China (CCP), Iran, and Venezuela, uses shared source codes, overseas servers, and psychological ops to install puppets and erode democracy.

From Huawei's espionage tools to Miru's "glitchy" exports, to Dominion's remote access flipping votes, the elite playbook is clear. Control the count, control the country. If we don't dismantle it, free elections are history. Who's next? Demand transparency.

data.raw_text:
The Iranian Women’s Football team is still in Australia right now, but the plan—under heavy regime pressure—is to return to Iran soon, likely routed through a third country like Turkey due to Middle East airspace closures from the recent conflict.

The team was eliminated from the AFC Women's Asian Cup 2026 today after a 2-0 loss to the Philippines in their final group match. Their Australian visas are valid until the end of March, but regime officials embedded with the squad are tightly controlling them: phones are monitored, players have reportedly been forced to sign promises not to seek asylum, and families back in Iran face punishment if anyone defects.

Iranian state TV has already labeled the players “war traitors” for the initial anthem protest, with threats of severe consequences upon return. Sources close to the team say seeking asylum in Australia “is not an option for most” precisely because of those family risks.

There’s a massive public push in Australia to stop them being sent back:
- An online petition has over 51,000 signatures calling on the government to provide protection, legal advice, and temporary safety.
- Opposition politicians (e.g. Julian Leeser) and Iranian-Australian activists are urging immediate humanitarian intervention.
- Foreign Minister Penny Wong has said Australia “stands in solidarity” but hasn’t confirmed any contact or offers of asylum.

As of right now (evening of March 8), no players have publicly sought or been granted asylum, and no defections have been reported. The most likely short-term scenario, according to multiple outlets tracking the situation, is that regime handlers will fly the squad home (via Turkey or similar) as soon as arrangements can be made—despite the danger and the calls for Australia to step in.
